title: What Makes a Modal Verb? Form and Core Features
brief: Define modal verbs as a closed set of auxiliary verbs (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would) and introduce the semi-modals (have to, need to, be able to, ought to). Explain the three key formal properties all modals share: they take no third-person singular -s (she can, not she cans), they are followed directly by a bare infinitive (must go, not must to go), and they form negatives and questions without do-support (can't you see? not do you can see?). Invent clear right/wrong example pairs to illustrate each property. Briefly note that semi-modals behave more like ordinary verbs and do require do-support and infinitive markers, setting up the contrast that will run through the unit.

title: Ability and Permission: Can, Could, and Be Able To
brief: Cover the two primary meanings carried by can and could — ability and permission — using invented example sentences for each (e.g., 'She can speak three languages' for present ability; 'He could swim before he started school' for past ability; 'Can I leave early today?' for informal permission). Explain that could functions as both the past form of can and as a more tentative or polite present/future form. Introduce be able to as the semi-modal alternative that fills the gaps where can has no form (e.g., future: 'will be able to'; perfect: 'has been able to'). Flag the common learner error of adding to after can ('I can to drive') and the confusion between could for past ability and could for polite requests.

title: Possibility and Probability: May, Might, and Could
brief: Explain that may, might, and could all express epistemic possibility — the speaker's assessment of how likely something is — but differ in degree of certainty. Present may as expressing a genuine open possibility ('It may rain this afternoon'), might as slightly more tentative or remote ('I might come to the party, but I'm not sure'), and could as flagging one option among several ('That noise could be the neighbours'). Invent a set of parallel example sentences so writers can show the contrast clearly. Address the common learner belief that may and might are completely interchangeable, and note the additional complication that may also carries a formal permission meaning, which can cause ambiguity. Exclude detailed discussion of past modals (might have, could have) as these belong to a later unit on perfect modal forms.

title: Obligation and Necessity: Must, Have To, and Should
brief: Distinguish between the three main ways English expresses obligation. Present must as expressing strong internal obligation or logical necessity, typically from the speaker's own authority or reasoning ('You must submit the form by Friday'; 'She must be tired — she's been working all day'). Contrast have to as expressing external obligation imposed by rules, laws, or circumstances ('I have to wear a uniform at work'). Introduce should and ought to as expressing weaker obligation or advice rather than strict necessity ('You should drink more water'). Invent classroom-relevant examples throughout. Highlight the major learner difficulty: must has no past tense form for obligation, so learners must use had to instead ('I had to stay late yesterday'), and confusing must not (prohibition) with don't have to (absence of obligation) is one of the most persistent errors at intermediate level.

title: Willingness, Prediction, and Politeness: Will, Would, and Shall
brief: Cover the range of meanings carried by will, would, and shall. Present will as the default future/prediction modal ('It will be cold tomorrow') and as expressing willingness or spontaneous decision ('I'll carry that for you'). Introduce would as the past form of will in reported speech ('She said she would call') and as the modal of hypothetical or polite contexts ('Would you like some coffee?'; 'I would move abroad if I could'). Address shall as largely restricted to formal British English for first-person offers and suggestions ('Shall I open the window?'; 'Shall we begin?') and note that learners from many language backgrounds rarely encounter shall in natural input. Flag the common error of using will in if-clauses of first conditional sentences ('If it will rain' instead of 'If it rains') and the confusion between would for past habit and used to, which is covered separately in the unit on aspect.

title: Teaching Modal Verbs: Typical Learner Difficulties and Classroom Strategies
brief: Synthesise the unit by mapping the most common learner difficulties onto practical classroom approaches. Identify four recurring problem areas: (1) adding to after modals, (2) applying third-person -s, (3) confusing must not with don't have to, and (4) treating modal meaning as one-to-one with the learner's L1 equivalent. Suggest using minimal-pair sentences to highlight meaning differences (e.g., 'You must not park here' versus 'You don't have to pay'), and recommend presenting modals grouped by meaning (ability, obligation, etc.) rather than one modal at a time, so learners build a network of contrasts. Invent two or three short dialogue examples that show modals in natural conversational context. Close by reminding teachers that because modals carry no inflection and resist simple rules, repeated exposure in meaningful contexts is more effective than isolated grammar drills.
